nameStory: The wrymouth gets its name from its distinctive twisted, wry-looking mouth that slants sharply upward at an odd angle. This unusual mouth position gives the fish a perpetually puzzled or crooked expression, as if it's constantly asking a question or making a wry comment about life on the seafloor.
description: The wrymouth is a slim, eel-like fish that looks like someone stretched a blenny into a long, skinny noodle. Despite its snake-like appearance, it can grow impressively large - up to 38 inches long, making it much bigger than its blenny relatives. Its most striking features are its oversized head with tiny eyes perched on top and that characteristic upward-slanting mouth that gives it such a distinctive appearance.

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: The mouth slants sharply upward above a heavy, prominent lower jaw, giving the fish a permanent 'wry' expression that's unmistakable once you see it

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Long, slim, and eel-like with a disproportionately large head - feels smooth and slippery when handled, like a wet snake

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: A single low dorsal fin runs the entire length of the back with about 70 small spines, connecting seamlessly with the tail and anal fins; completely lacks pelvic fins

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Reddish-brown upper body decorated with several irregular rows of small dark spots that also speckle the dorsal and anal fins

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Can reach up to 38 inches long, making it substantially larger than most other eel-like fish you'll encounter in New England waters

habitat: Wrymouths inhabit deeper offshore waters along New England's continental shelf, typically found on muddy or sandy bottoms where they can burrow and hide. They prefer cooler waters and are most commonly encountered by commercial fishermen working deeper areas, rarely coming into shallow coastal waters where recreational anglers might find them.

seasonality.spring: May be more active as waters warm, though deep-water habitat means seasonal changes are less pronounced than for shallow-water species.
seasonality.summer: Found in their typical deep-water habitats; any specimens brought up by fishing vessels will show their characteristic features clearly.
seasonality.fall: Continues normal deep-water behavior with little visible seasonal change in appearance or activity patterns.
seasonality.winter: Remains in deeper waters where temperatures stay relatively stable throughout the cold months.

funFact: The wrymouth is sometimes called the 'ghostfish' because of its pale, almost translucent appearance when brought up from the deep, and it can actually burrow tail-first into soft sediment, disappearing completely except for that weird upward-pointing mouth sticking out like a periscope!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with eels, but the wrymouth's upward-slanting mouth and continuous dorsal fin starting right behind the head are dead giveaways. Remember: if the mouth points up like it's asking 'why me?', it's a wrymouth!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'ghostfish' or even 'potato-head fish' by some fishermen, the wrymouth is actually not closely related to true eels - it's more like an oversized, deep-water blenny that decided to go eel-shaped for life in the depths.
compareHints: The wrymouth is the only species in its genus found in New England waters, making it unique in its family. Compared to similar eel-like fish in the region, it's distinguished by its much larger size, the distinctive upward-slanting mouth, and the complete absence of pelvic fins - features that set it apart from both true eels and other elongated fish species.
